newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Shell Singapore to cut output if losses continue.
newsitem.headline: Shell Singapore to cut output if losses continue.

text.p: Shell Singapore, Singapore's largest oil refiner, said on Monday it would reduce output if the refining losses persisted.
"If the current margin squeeze continues, our refinery runs will be reduced," a Shell spokeswoman told Reuters.
Industry sources said Singapore refiners were losing about 50 cents on each barrel of crude refined at the basic stage of refining, compared to profits of more than $2.00 in April.
Shell, which has a refining capacity of 435,000 barrels per day (bpd), dominates the Singapore oil sector, which has a total capacity of nearly 1.3 million bpd.

Singapore refiners incurred losess for the first time in four months in mid-May and were expected to cut their output within the next few weeks if product prices do not pick up, industry sources said.
Margins slipped into the red after crude prices rose over the past three weeks at the same time as oil product prices fell in the face of poor regional demand.
The refiners in Singapore, the swing producers of Asia, are looked upon as a bell-weather for the state of the industry in this region.
Refining sources said the companies would cut output once they have sorted out their crude and product commitments.
"It depend on the product inventory level and commitment of crude," a refining source said. "It takes time for the refinery to react."
But the reaction time to losses have been reduced considerably over the past few years as tough market conditions have forced them to be more lean, industry sources said.
In January, it took the refiners less than two weeks to decide on a need to cut crude runs.
Then, Shell Singapore reduced output by 30,000 bpd for about one month when refining losses plunged to a low of up to $2.00 per barrel.
This time, the refiners are not entirely convinced that the current bearish market will last for long, one source said. That was why the refiners were hesitatant about in cutting output.
Traders said the refiners might be hoping for fresh regional demand, especially for fuel oil, diesel and gasoline -- products which are in high demand during the summer -- to lift prices.
But most refining sources said the more flexible refiners would cut output in the next one or two weeks if losses continued.
